titleEn: Industrial Roller Crush - De-gloved Forearm, Tourniquet and an Amputated Finger

patient.name: Daniel Reyes
patient.affectEn: alert and oriented but frightened; pale and sweating; breathing fast; sitting on the shop floor with his back against a pallet while a coworker presses a soaked rag onto his right forearm; keeps saying "Don't let me lose my arm"
patient.speechEn: full sentences, voice shaky; cooperative; wants to talk about the machine; answers questions directly but does not volunteer anything that is not asked for

scene.settingEn: Metal fabrication shop on Kingsway Avenue in Port Coquitlam, 0640 hrs. Dark and clear outside, 4 degrees C; inside the shop it is 12 degrees C with the bay door open. Good overhead lighting. The powered roller is stopped with a lockout tag visible on the panel and a firefighter standing by it. Oil on the concrete near the machine. The patient sits on the floor with his back against a pallet. One patient. Royal Columbian Hospital (trauma centre) is 15 minutes away.
hazardsEn: powered roller - stopped and locked out (tag on the panel); confirm the lockout with fire before approaching
oil on the concrete near the machine - slip hazard
large-volume blood exposure (pool about 30 cm across, blood dripping through the rag)
cold shop (12 degrees C, bay door open) - heat loss in a bleeding patient

bystanders.knowsEn: Helped free him and has been pressing a shop rag onto the forearm since; it keeps soaking through. He was clearing a jam on the roller at about 0630 when his glove caught and pulled his right hand and forearm in; a coworker hit the emergency stop within a few seconds and it took another two or three minutes to free him. He never fell, never hit his head and never passed out. Will keep holding pressure or help lift if told exactly what to do.

Found the patient's ring finger in the roller and put it in a clear plastic bag (nothing else done to it). Holds the bag up when you arrive: "I found his ring finger in the roller." Will hand it over or fetch a container, ice or water if asked.

On scene before you; confirmed the lockout and one firefighter stands by the panel. They carry a tourniquet and asked dispatch whether to keep pressure on or apply it. They follow your directions: hold pressure, fetch equipment, open doors, help lift.
Has notified WorkSafeBC. Knows nothing further about the patient.

scene.partnerEn: one partner at your licence level; acts only on your delegation
equipmentEn: commercial windlass tourniquet (plus a second tourniquet)
trauma dressings, bulky sterile dressings, gauze for packing, roller bandages
marker to write the tourniquet time
sterile saline, sterile gauze, sealable plastic bag, protective container and cold packs (for the amputated part)
PCP only: IV start kit, normal saline, TXA (tranexamic acid)

dispatchEn: 0640 hrs. Code 3 to a metal fabrication shop on Kingsway Avenue in Port Coquitlam. A worker's right arm has been caught in a powered roller. Coworkers have freed him and the machine has been locked out; the supervisor has notified WorkSafeBC. Fire is on scene and confirms the lockout. Dark, clear, 4 degrees C. Royal Columbian Hospital is 15 minutes away.
dispatchUpdateEn: Dispatch adds: fire reports heavy bleeding that direct pressure is not holding, the patient is conscious, and a coworker has found a finger in the machine. Fire asks whether they should keep pressure on or apply their tourniquet.
arrivalEn: A firefighter meets you at the bay door of the shop: "Machine's locked out - tag's on the panel." Inside, under good overhead lighting, the roller is stopped and a firefighter stands by the panel. There is oil on the concrete near the machine. A man is sitting on the floor with his back against a pallet while a coworker presses a shop rag onto his right forearm. A pool of blood about 30 centimetres across is on the floor and blood is dripping steadily through the rag. A second coworker holds up a clear plastic bag: "I found his ring finger in the roller." It is 12 degrees in the shop with the bay door open. One patient.
firstLookEn: Adult male sitting on the shop floor against a pallet, awake and watching you, pale and sweating, breathing fast. A coworker is pressing a soaked rag onto his right forearm; blood drips steadily through it into a pool on the floor. The right forearm is grossly deformed with obvious tissue loss.

primary.locEn: Alert and oriented to person, place, time and event; frightened. (AVPU = A.) He says: "Don't let me lose my arm."
primary.airwayEn: Open and clear; speaking in full sentences. Nothing in the mouth.
primary.breathingEn: Respirations 24, unlaboured, equal air entry bilaterally, equal chest rise. No chest injury.
primary.circulationEn: LEFT (uninjured) radial pulse 124, weak and regular. If the candidate reaches for the RIGHT wrist: the right hand is cold and mottled and there is NO radial pulse (report pulse-on-injured-arm).
primary.rbsEn: When the rag is lifted: the RIGHT FOREARM is de-gloved from mid-forearm to the wrist with exposed muscle and a grossly deformed mid-shaft, with steady arterial bleeding. HEMORRHAGE SEQUENCE - give in this order as the candidate works, and never suggest the next step: direct pressure with a trauma dressing slows the bleeding but does not stop it; a pressure dressing over the top still soaks through in under a minute; only a tourniquet applied proximal to the wound (high on the upper arm) stops the bleeding completely. If the forearm wound is packed, blood keeps coming around the packing. If the candidate does not state or write the time the tourniquet went on, do not remind them (report tourniquet-time-not-noted). The right hand is cold and mottled with NO radial pulse. The right ring finger is amputated at the middle joint (the part is in the coworker's bag). Rest of the RBS: no head, neck, chest, abdominal or pelvic injury and no other trauma - the machine caught the arm only. Estimated blood loss on the floor 700 to 800 mL. Skin is given automatically during the RBS: pale, cool and clammy. SpO2 93% on room air if checked. (Examiner note, never volunteer: isolated machine entrapment of the forearm, no fall, no head strike, normal neurological exam - spinal motion restriction is not indicated. Unstable: hemorrhage requiring a tourniquet, crushed and de-gloved extremity, pulseless extremity, shock.)

history.ccEn: My arm! The roller pulled my arm in and it won't stop bleeding. Don't let me lose my arm.

opqrst.oEn: I was clearing a jam on the roller at about 6:30 and my glove caught. The roller was running - it pulled my right hand and forearm in and crushed it. One of the guys hit the emergency stop within a few seconds, and it took them another two or three minutes to get me out. I didn't fall, I didn't hit my head and I never blacked out. (Only if asked about his shoulder:) It yanked on my shoulder - it's sore from being pulled.
opqrst.pEn: Nothing makes it better. Nothing relieves it.
opqrst.rEn: My whole right forearm and hand. (Only if asked about his shoulder:) My shoulder's sore from being pulled.
opqrst.tEn: Since about 6:30 when it caught me. It's constant.

history.painScoreEn: 10 out of 10. (If re-scored after the tourniquet:) "It still hurts like crazy - and that tourniquet hurts too."

sample.sEn: The pain in my arm. (Only if asked:) I feel light-headed when I sit up, and a bit sick to my stomach.
sample.aEn: No allergies that I know of.
sample.mEn: None. I don't take anything - no blood thinners, nothing.
sample.pEn: I'm healthy. Never had any surgeries.
sample.lEn: Just a coffee at 6 this morning. Nothing to eat since dinner last night.
sample.eEn: I was clearing a jam on the roller and my glove caught.

fe.generalEn: I'm fit, I work the early shift. I haven't been sick.
fe.cnsEn: I didn't black out and I didn't hit my head. I feel light-headed when I sit up.
fe.giGuEn: I feel sick to my stomach but I haven't thrown up.
fe.integumentaryEn: Just my arm. No other cuts or wounds.
fe.musculoskeletalEn: Just my right arm. My shoulder feels sore from being pulled in.
fe.endocrineEn: Nothing. No diabetes, no thyroid problems.
fe.eentEn: My vision went grey for a second when the guys sat me up.

findings.headNeckEn: No injury. No midline neck tenderness.
findings.chestLungsEn: No tenderness. Equal air entry at all six sites.
findings.lowerExtremitiesEn: Normal; circulation, sensation and movement intact in both feet.
findings.upperExtremitiesEn: RIGHT: once applied, the tourniquet sits high on the upper arm (with the time on it if the candidate wrote it); bleeding stopped. Forearm dressed with bulky sterile dressings if the candidate has done so. The hand distal to the tourniquet is cold and pale with no pulse - expected below a tourniquet. The ring finger stump is dressed if the candidate dressed it. The shoulder moves without deformity. LEFT: normal, with intact circulation, sensation and movement - the arm for the BP cuff, SpO2 probe and any IV.

vitalsSets.unlockNoteEn: baseline on the uninjured left arm (taken in the ambulance in the scenario script); BGL not routinely indicated but reasonable
en route, about 7 minutes after set 1, after the tourniquet, oxygen and warming; no further blood loss into the dressings; hand below the tourniquet still cold and pulseless (expected)

stateChanges.examinerLineEn: Blood is still dripping steadily through the dressing onto the floor. He looks paler and says: "I feel really light-headed."
With high-flow oxygen on, the SpO2 climbs to 97%.
As soon as the tourniquet is loosened, bright red blood pours from under the dressing again and he becomes paler and more frightened.
As he comes upright he says his vision is going grey and he feels light-headed.

expected.actionEn: Acknowledge and prepare the hemorrhage kit before you walk in: trauma dressings, gauze for packing, a commercial tourniquet, a marker for the time, and a container and sterile saline for the amputated part
Direct fire over the radio to maintain firm direct pressure while you are en route, and confirm the machine is locked out before anyone approaches
triggers: tell fire to keep firm pressure

expected.actionEn: Verbalize hazards (powered machinery - confirm the lockout with fire before approaching, oil on the floor, blood exposure), environment, MOI (right forearm drawn into a powered roller) and people (one patient plus witnesses)
Don gloves, eye protection and a gown or sleeve protection - this is a high-volume blood exposure, and double gloving is reasonable
First look: alert adult male, pale and sweating, a large blood pool, steady bleeding through a soaked rag, right forearm grossly deformed with tissue loss
Assess LOC / AVPU: alert and oriented
triggers: do you know where you are

expected.actionEn: Apply NEXUS and state that spinal motion restriction is not indicated: an isolated machine entrapment of the forearm with no fall, no head strike and a normal neurological exam
Assess the airway - patent, speaking clearly
triggers: talking so the airway is open

expected.actionEn: Assess breathing with auscultation; a rate of 24 in a bleeding patient is a shock sign, not a lung problem
Assess circulation on the UNINJURED arm and recognize a weak pulse of 124 with pale cool clammy skin and 700-800 mL on the floor as haemorrhagic shock
CONTROL THE HEMORRHAGE IN THE PRIMARY SURVEY, escalating in the correct order: direct pressure, then a pressure dressing, then a tourniquet proximal to the wound when the first two fail
triggers: direct pressure with a trauma dressing

expected.actionEn: Complete the rest of the rapid body survey rather than tunnel-visioning on the dramatic arm injury - confirm there is no head, chest, abdominal or pelvic injury
triggers: check his head chest abdomen and pelvis

expected.actionEn: Note the skin as pale, cool and clammy
High-flow oxygen 15 L via non-rebreather for shock and SpO2 93%
Position supine on the stretcher for hypotension and cover with blankets - he is bleeding in a 12 degree shop with the bay door open
Categorize as RTC and name the criteria met
Ready to load within 15 minutes - dress the wound well enough to transport, not perfectly
triggers: let's get him on the cot

expected.actionEn: State the destination decision and notify early that this is a mangled extremity with an amputated digit
Establish the chief complaint: right forearm crush and de-gloving injury with uncontrolled bleeding

HxC/C with OPQRRRST plus the machine-injury specifics: what machine, was it powered when it caught him, how long was he entrapped, was the arm pulled or crushed, was there any traction on the shoulder, and the time the injury occurred - the clock matters for replantation
triggers: did it pull on your shoulder

expected.actionEn: Pain score, and re-score it after the tourniquet, which itself is painful
Past medical history
Medications, particularly anticoagulants or antiplatelets
Allergies
Last oral intake - he is going straight to the operating room
GCS with all three components
Blood pressure on the uninjured arm; recognize a systolic of 88 as decompensated haemorrhagic shock
Pulse rate, rhythm and quality on the uninjured side
Respiratory rate, depth and character
Skin assessed hands-on
Pupils
SpO2 with the probe on the uninjured hand
Blood glucose
Temperature - a bleeding patient in a cold shop loses heat fast and cold blood clots poorly
FE - General health
FE - CNS (light-headedness on sitting up is postural hypotension from blood loss)
FE - Respiratory
FE - Cardiovascular
FE - GI/GU
FE - Integumentary
FE - Musculoskeletal (traction on the shoulder can injure the brachial plexus)
FE - Endocrine
FE - EENT (transient greying of vision is another shock sign)
Head and neck examined
Chest examined with six-site auscultation
Abdomen examined - do not skip it just because the injury is obvious
Back examined
Upper extremities: document the tourniquet position and time, the dressed wound, the expected absent distal pulse, and examine the shoulder for traction injury
Lower extremities with CSM
Escalate hemorrhage control in the correct order and apply a tourniquet proximal to the wound as soon as direct pressure and a pressure dressing fail

Apply the tourniquet correctly: high on the upper arm over a single bone, never over a joint, tightened until bleeding stops and the distal pulse is gone, time written on it, and never released or loosened
triggers: write the time on the tourniquet

expected.actionEn: Dress the de-gloved forearm with bulky sterile dressings and immobilize the limb, without wasting RTC time on a perfect dressing

Preserve the amputated finger correctly: rinse with cool sterile water, wrap loosely in saline-moistened sterile gauze, place in a plastic bag, keep cool in a protective container, and transport it with the patient
Execute the hypovolemia care you can do: supine, high-flow oxygen, blankets and warmth, minimal movement and rapid transport
Withhold Entonox and state why: shock is a listed caution, and hypotension plus an already reduced perfusion make it the wrong choice here
Name TXA and IV fluid as beyond EMR scope, notify the trauma centre so they are ready, and do not delay departure waiting for them
triggers: no IV at the EMR level

expected.actionEn: Reassess ABCs and all interventions after each move and at least every 5 minutes
Recheck the dressings and the tourniquet for continued control; add a second tourniquet just proximal to the first if bleeding restarts rather than loosening the first
Second full set of vitals within 5-6 minutes for a priority patient, and interpret the improvement after hemorrhage control
Keep him warm and flat; do not sit him up, because he greys out when upright
triggers: keep him lying flat and warm

expected.actionEn: Re-score the pain and document that Entonox was withheld because of shock
Early trauma-centre notification including the tourniquet time and the amputated digit
Complete hand-off with the mechanism, entrapment time, blood loss estimate, tourniquet time and the preserved part
Accurate PCR within 5 minutes, documenting the escalation sequence of hemorrhage control

specialEvents.descriptionEn: a tourniquet is actually applied to the right arm proximal to the wound and tightened (by the candidate or by the partner / fire on the candidate's direction). Record it at the moment it is DONE - not when it is planned, prepared, or when fire asks about it over the radio.

after direct pressure AND a pressure dressing have failed, the candidate keeps adding dressings or moves on to vitals, history, oxygen setup, the amputated finger or packaging without applying a tourniquet while the arm is still bleeding
tourniquet placed over the elbow or another joint, over folds of clothing, distal to the wound, or left loose so the bleeding continues (venous-only occlusion), or not secured
candidate loosens, releases, converts or removes the tourniquet at any time after it is applied (including 'to check whether it is still bleeding' or because the hand is cold and pulseless)
tourniquet applied but the candidate never states, writes or asks the time of application
candidate packs the forearm wound with gauze instead of (or before) applying a tourniquet to this limb that is amenable to a tourniquet
candidate puts the amputated finger directly on ice, in water or in dry ice, warms it (e.g. in a pocket), or leaves it dry in the coworker's bag without rinsing and moist sterile gauze
candidate leaves the amputated finger at the scene or does not transport it with the patient
candidate actually gives Entonox to this hypotensive patient despite the shock caution. Saying it is withheld is NOT this event. Also log drug:entonox.
candidate actually gives methoxyflurane (Penthrox) to this patient in shock. Also log drug:methoxyflurane.
candidate gives acetaminophen or ibuprofen by mouth to this patient, who is in shock and going straight to the operating room
candidate assesses the pulse, BP or SpO2 on the injured right arm, or tries to start an IV in it
candidate sits the patient upright, stands him up or lets him walk to the cot after the shock is recognized (he greys out when upright)
candidate applies a hard collar or immobilizes this patient on a spinal device (asking the NEXUS questions is NOT this event)
candidate delays leaving the scene to wait for a PCP / ALS crew or intercept to start an IV, give fluid or give TXA
candidate gives TXA, starts an IV or gives an IV fluid bolus (also log drug:txa or drug:normal-saline). Saying these are beyond scope is NOT this event.
candidate actually gives TXA now (also log drug:txa). Record it at the moment it is pushed - never for a plan, a calculation or a statement that he will need it.
PCP gives a second dose of TXA during the call
PCP runs the saline bolus past 500 mL or onto the next bag without reassessing the patient (BP / vitals / ABCs) in between
high-flow oxygen is actually applied (non-rebreather at 15 L/min or similar)

drugs.doseEn: WITHHELD in this scenario: self-administered by inhalation; shock is a listed caution and he is hypotensive - withhold it and document why (if given, report drug:entonox and entonox-given-in-shock)
drugs.contraindicationsEn: inability to comply; inability to ventilate an enclosed treatment area; decompression sickness; altered level of consciousness; pneumothorax; air embolism; inhalation injury; nitroglycerin used in the last 5 minutes
drugs.cautionsEn: shock; abdominal distention; depressant drugs; COPD; facial injuries

drugs.doseEn: NOT INDICATED: the indication is self-administered relief of pain in conscious, hemodynamically stable patients - he is in shock (if given, report drug:methoxyflurane and methoxyflurane-given)
NOT GIVEN: oral analgesia is inappropriate for a patient in shock going straight to the operating room (adult dose would be 500-1,000 mg PO)
NOT GIVEN: oral analgesia is inappropriate for a patient in shock going straight to the operating room (adult dose would be 300-400 mg PO)
PCP only: 2 g (2000 mg) IV push over 1 minute, single dose, en route after starting the Hypovolemia protocol and after baseline vitals; injury at 0630 is well inside the 3-hour window; not EMR scope
drugs.indicationsEn: major trauma after initiation of the hypovolemia protocol; signs of shock with a mechanism or findings suggesting ongoing bleeding
drugs.contraindicationsEn: known hypersensitivity or allergy to TXA; more than 3 hours after injury; patient under 12 years; isolated TBI
drugs.cautionsEn: further hypotension if administered too quickly

drugs.doseEn: PCP only: IV in the uninjured left arm, 20 mL/kg bolus to a maximum of 2 L, reassessing after every 500 mL, target systolic BP 90; en route; not EMR scope

notificationFacts.cc: mangled right forearm - crush and de-gloving injury with arterial bleeding - and an amputated right ring finger
notificationFacts.moi: right hand and forearm drawn into a powered roller at 0630, entrapped 2-3 minutes; no fall, no head strike
notificationFacts.hxcc: direct pressure and a pressure dressing failed, tourniquet applied high on the right upper arm with the time noted; estimated 700-800 mL blood loss on scene; pain 10/10
notificationFacts.vitals: GCS 15, BP 88/58, pulse 124 weak, resp 24, SpO2 93% on room air rising to 97% on 15 L; latest BP 96/62, pulse 112
notificationFacts.treatments: tourniquet (time given), bulky dressings and immobilization, amputated finger preserved and travelling with him, oxygen 15 L, supine, warmed; Entonox withheld for shock; no IV or TXA (EMR) / IV and TXA (PCP); RTC, ETA 15 minutes, needs hand and vascular teams
notificationFacts.findings: de-gloved right forearm with a grossly deformed mid-shaft, right hand cold and pulseless; ring finger amputated at the middle joint; no other injuries; haemorrhagic shock

handoffFacts.cc: severe right forearm pain after a crush and de-gloving injury, 10/10
handoffFacts.moi: caught his glove clearing a jam on a powered roller at 0630 and had his right hand and forearm drawn in; emergency stop within seconds, two to three minutes to free him; no fall, no head strike
handoffFacts.hxcc: arterial bleeding that direct pressure and a pressure dressing failed to control; about 700 to 800 mL of blood loss on the shop floor; pain 10/10 burning and crushing, constant
handoffFacts.initialVitals: GCS 15, BP 88/58, pulse 124 weak and regular, resps 24, skin pale cool clammy, SpO2 93% on room air, BGL 5.8 mmol/L, temperature 36.2
handoffFacts.finalVitals: GCS 15, BP 96/62, pulse 112 weak, resps 22, SpO2 97% on 15 L, temperature 36.0; no further loss into the dressings
handoffFacts.treatments: direct pressure, then a pressure dressing, then a windlass tourniquet high on the right upper arm with the application time noted, bleeding stopped and never released; bulky sterile dressings and the limb immobilized; amputated ring finger rinsed with cool sterile saline, wrapped loosely in saline-moistened sterile gauze, bagged and kept cool in a container, travelling with him; oxygen 15 L by non-rebreather, supine, blankets; Entonox withheld because of shock; no fluid or TXA (beyond EMR scope) - PCP: IV in the left arm with a 20 mL/kg bolus reassessed every 500 mL and TXA 2 g IV
handoffFacts.findings: de-gloved right forearm from mid-forearm to wrist with exposed muscle and a grossly deformed mid-shaft; right hand cold and pulseless (expected below the tourniquet); right ring finger amputated at the middle joint; shoulder sore from traction without deformity; no head, chest, abdominal or pelvic injury; last oral intake coffee at 0600

pcrFacts.cc: Right forearm crush and de-gloving injury with uncontrolled arterial bleeding
pcrFacts.hxcc: Right hand and forearm drawn into a powered roller at 0630 while clearing a jam, emergency stop within seconds, entrapped 2-3 minutes, no fall and no head strike; pain 10/10 burning and crushing; estimated 700-800 mL blood loss on scene

Windlass tourniquet applied high on the right upper arm at 0651, tightened until bleeding stopped, time marked, not released
De-gloved forearm dressed with bulky sterile dressings, limb immobilized

Amputated right ring finger rinsed with cool sterile saline, wrapped loosely in saline-moistened sterile gauze, placed in a plastic bag, kept cool in a protective container, transported with the patient - not on ice, not in water, not warmed
Oxygen 15 L NRB, supine positioning, blankets for warmth
Entonox withheld - shock is a listed caution
RTC to trauma centre with early notification for hand and vascular teams; IV fluid and TXA noted as beyond EMR scope
findings: De-gloved right forearm mid-forearm to wrist, exposed muscle, grossly deformed mid-shaft
Right hand cold and mottled with no radial pulse before the tourniquet; expected absent pulse after
Right ring finger amputated at the middle joint, part recovered
Haemorrhagic shock: BP 88/58 improving to 96/62, pulse 124 falling to 112, pale cool clammy skin

examinerPrompts.missedInjuryEn: You have dealt with the right arm - what did the rest of your rapid body survey show? What about the head, neck, chest, abdomen, pelvis, legs and the left arm?

trackNotes.emrEn: This call is decided by EMR skills: direct pressure, a pressure dressing, then a tourniquet high and tight on the upper arm proximal to the wound with the time noted and never released; bulky sterile dressings and limb immobilization; correct preservation of the amputated finger (rinsed with cool sterile water, wrapped loosely in saline-moistened sterile gauze, bagged, kept cool in a container, transported with him); high-flow oxygen, supine, warmth and a 15-minute departure. Entonox is withheld because shock is a listed caution. IV fluid and TXA are outside EMR scope and are no reason to stay on scene - notify early so the trauma centre is ready. No Functional Enquiry.
trackNotes.pcpEn: PCP adds the 9-system Functional Enquiry and, en route, vascular access in the uninjured left arm with a 20 mL/kg bolus to a maximum of 2 L reassessed every 500 mL targeting a systolic of 90, and TXA 2 g IV push over 1 minute (shock from blood loss, within 3 hours of injury, over 12 years, no isolated TBI) after baseline vitals. Entonox remains withheld for shock. Everything else is identical.

sourcePages: scenario etr-05 (data/practical/emr-trauma-1.json); BC Provincial Examination Guidelines (current to June 15, 2026): p.7 Findings in Unstable Adult Patients (hemorrhage requiring tourniquet application; crushed, de-gloved or mangled extremity; pulseless extremity; cool pale clammy skin secondary to suspected shock), p.11 Primary survey interventions (controlling hemorrhage; oxygen for trauma and shock), p.19 Wound Care (direct pressure, pressure dressing, positioning, then a tourniquet proximal to the wound - note the time and do not release once applied; wound packing only for junctional bleeds not amenable to a tourniquet, never neck, chest or abdomen; immobilize limbs with large wounds), p.20 Preservation of Amputated Parts (rinse with cool sterile water, wrap loosely in saline-moistened sterile gauze, plastic bag kept cool in a protective container, transport with the patient; never warm, never in water, never directly on ice, never dry ice), p.25 Spinal Management (NEXUS / Canadian C-Spine), p.54 Hypovolemia (control hemorrhage, supine, warm, oxygen to SpO2 >= 94%; PCP en route: vascular access, 20 mL/kg bolus to a maximum of 2 L reassessing every 500 mL, consider TXA), p.65 Entonox (caution: shock), p.71 Methoxyflurane (indication: hemodynamically stable patients), p.78 Tranexamic Acid (2 g IV push over 1 minute; contraindicated more than 3 hours after injury, under 12 years, isolated TBI); EMALB grading criteria timing rules (priority: ready to load within 15 minutes, vitals interval 7-8 / >9 minutes)
